name: CR-Diff-07-implicit-1.b
questiontext:
Find \(\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}\) in terms of {{CT:1}} when \(x\) and {{CT:1}} are related by the following equation:

\[x = {{CT:2}}\]

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
generalfeedback:
\[x={{CT:2}}\] So,

\[\frac{dx}{dx}=2{{CT:0}}\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}-\frac{1}{{{CT:0}}^2}\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx} \] So, taking common factor \(\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}\),

\[1=\left(2{{CT:0}} -\frac{1}{{{CT:0}}^2}\right)\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}\] Hence,

\[\begin{array}{rcl}\displaystyle
  \frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx} &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{1}{2{{CT:0}} -\frac{1}{{{CT:0}}^2}} \\
   &\displaystyle =&\displaystyle  \frac{{{CT:0}}^2}{2{{CT:0}}^3+1}
 \end{array}\]

on_true.feedback:
Your answer is the negative of what it should be.

Have you mislaid a sign?

You have found \(\frac{dx}{d{{CT:0}}}\) not \(\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}\).

To get \(\frac{dx}{d{{CT:0}}}\) use the chain ule to get \(\frac{1}{\frac{d{{CT:0}}}{dx}}\).

You appear to have used {@q@} instead of {{CT:3}}.

The method looks fine but take care of the signs.
